Seven products.

The experiment, in public

Small tools. Real learning.

Seven free, open-source launches. One experiment: turn AI work into useful tools people can keep improving.

Useful by design.

Start with a recurring need. Build with AI, test with people, then maintain a tool others can use.

Yours to take further.

Improve the MIT code with Astra or your AI: a clear brief, your budget, guided iterations and real tests. Share what you learn or submit a reviewed PR.

Honest about cost.

Often hundreds, not pocket change. Build budgets and model stacks stay illustrative until I publish the actuals.

SaaS is dead.

Own the workflow. Question the recurring bill.

CHO.

One accountable lead. Tools for the whole team.

The experiment continues

Shipping is the start.
Feedback is what follows.

In the days after launch, I’ll consider every bug report, request and suggestion. I’ll weigh the value, the smallest useful change and the AI-compute cost, then do my best to fund quick iterations myself.

01 · Listen to real use

Tell me what broke, what got in your way, or what could make the project more useful.

02 · Fix what matters

Bugs first. Then meaningful, manageable improvements rather than a growing list of half-built features.

03 · Improve it together

Use public feedback to choose the next iteration, and be open about progress, limits and cost.

Every request considered. Not every feature promised, and no guaranteed turnaround. Share feedback through the project’s repository or the launch conversation.
Web Summit Lisbon · 9–12 November

Let’s meet at Web Summit.

I’ll be at Web Summit in Lisbon from 9 to 12 November as a VIP attendee, on my own: no booth, just conversations. It runs alongside the first four days of the Weekathon, which I dedicate to Web Summit and the builders’ mentality. Meet me there, or informally around Lisbon, where I live.

Enki needs more talent, reach and resources than any one founder can bring: I’ll help in year one, then step away. And I’m raising funds for Openline, my main startup, to reshape the eSIM market with a deep pipeline of ideas ready to execute, so investors are welcome to talk about that too.

I’d love to meet

Unlocked for this session

About this budget

An approximation, not a price.

This figure adds up the AI tokens consumed and the hours spent across every iteration, along with any other computing, marketing or hosting costs.

It is an approximate total for each project, not a product price or an invoice. Example tools and models shown on the cards remain unconfirmed.

SaaS is dead.

Rent by default? Not anymore.

My bet is that more companies will build and own the workflows they used to rent. But swapping SaaS seats for endless AI calls misses the point. Use AI to create reusable tools, then make every recurring cost earn its place.

For companies

Replacing subscriptions with an uncontrolled AI bill isn't sovereignty. I want a CHO to turn repeated prompts into owned apps, use ordinary code for predictable steps, and test small self-hosted models for narrow jobs. Compare cost per successful result, including hardware, power, hosting, licences, security, maintenance and human time. Self-hosting is not automatically cheaper or private.

For SaaS founders and investors

My deliberately aggressive belief: AI can already reproduce the software functionality of any SaaS company's entire product line, small or large, for less than one month of its revenue. Soon, perhaps sooner than we expect, I think that budget could fall to one customer's annual bill, then eventually their monthly bill. If I'm right, SaaS economics built only on reproducible features could be reduced to dust. This is my prediction, not an industry benchmark. Recreating software is not rebuilding proprietary data, infrastructure, compliance or customer trust.

Software on demand. Responsibility included.

Build where ownership creates an advantage. Keep paying where a supplier delivers value you cannot sensibly reproduce. This Weekathon is a public experiment, not proof that every subscription should disappear.

What is a Chief Hacking Officer?

Why “hacking”?

Think life hacks and biohacks: finding a smarter route through a problem, not just cybersecurity. Shortcuts through friction, not around consent, security or quality.

A Chief Hacking Officer uses AI to make an organisation work faster and better: sovereign software, reusable workflows and tools people can maintain. One accountable lead or small team, backed by the right experts. You don't need to be a founder to grow into the role.

AI + the right people

Centralise ownership, budgets and evaluation, not every decision. Work with internal specialists and expert contractors. Keep useful AI access available, define permissions and make handoffs real. A CHO enables engineering, sales, marketing, legal and operations; nobody replaces all their expertise.

Build with AI. Run with judgement.

Turn repeated prompts into reusable workflows. Use ordinary code for predictable steps. Test small models for bounded tasks and bigger models for genuine gaps. Measure quality and full cost, including upkeep and human review. The deliverable is a supported tool with an owner, not a chat transcript.

A useful comparison: Paysend's CEO describes selective AI trials, expansion after measurable value, and a shared internal coding agent. Not a blanket ban to cut costs. Read the Paysend CEO interview

One home for your code

Put every tool’s code, tests, documentation and deployment recipes in organisation-owned Git repositories: GitHub, GitLab or, preferably, a self-hosted/local forge. One governed source of truth, with access controls, backups and mirrors, not one fragile server. Keep secrets and personal data out.

Private where needed. Open where useful.

Publish as much reusable, non-sensitive code as rights and security allow. Keep critical internals private. Clear licences, tests and documented releases let other organisations improve a shared foundation instead of rebuilding it.

Fork evidence, not promises.

Give your teams and AI assistants reviewed code, test results and known limitations to build on. Fork a relevant release, adapt it, validate it in your context and send useful improvements upstream. A shared starting point for people and AI-assisted work, not automatic proof of safety.

Tools you could ship

Start with a recurring bottleneck. These are examples, not a promise to build everything.

Marketing

Campaign landing pages, experiment dashboards and reusable creative workflows.

Sales

Proposal builders, account-research tools and CRM handoff automations.

Operations

Onboarding portals, approval flows, vendor tracking and internal dashboards.

Engineering

Release tooling, QA assistants, incident runbooks and developer utilities.

Legal

Contract intake, clause libraries and review workflows, with legal professionals owning the judgement.

Social media

Editorial calendars, draft libraries, approval queues and performance dashboards. Humans approve what gets published.

Public releases

Customer-facing apps, small utilities and selected open-source projects, with a real owner for support and improvements.

Impact, not output volume

Aim for less repetitive work, better handoffs and tools teams can maintain. Measure the result, include the full running cost, and keep testing, security and human approval in scope. Often the right decision is to build, own and keep it sovereign.

A playful title. Serious about consulting.

A great company or ambitious startup, a worthwhile product, mutual trust and a modest budget? I'm open to a consulting CHO role of up to 30 hours a week. Bring a real problem and a mandate, and message me on LinkedIn.

My personal split is roughly 100 hours a week: 60 for Openline, up to 30 for consulting, and 10 for personal ventures such as Cup of News and Enki. My choice, not an expectation for your team. Consulting is separate from Openline's fundraising.
